Read
rēd
v.t. (rendering Hebrew qara', Greek anaginōskō)
From Saxon raedan, to counsel, to discern, to read — the same root as our rede, counsel. Hebrew qara' means first to call or cry aloud, and reading in Israel was reading out; Greek anaginōskō is literally to know again, to recognise, since to read is to take back up a knowledge someone has already set down.

Biblical Definition

Reading in Scripture is a public and covenantal act before it is a private one. When the exiles returned, the great scene of reformation is a reading: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8) — the text read out, and then explained, which is the whole pattern of preaching in one verse. The king of Israel was bound to the same discipline for himself: “he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God” (Deuteronomy 17:19) — the crown does not exempt a man from the book, it binds him to it. Our Lord kept the practice without apology: “as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read” (Luke 4:16). And when a foreign official was found reading Isaiah in a chariot, the Spirit sent a preacher to him with one question: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Acts 8:30) — a question that assumes the text has a sense, that the sense can be missed, and that God supplies men to give it. To read the Scriptures is therefore not to gather information; it is to be summoned, and the fear of the LORD is the stated aim.

Webster 1828 Definition

To peruse and understand written characters; to utter aloud what is written; in Scripture, the public reading of the law with the sense given, the king's daily reading that he might learn to fear the LORD, and the eunuch asked whether he understood what he read.

expand to see more

READ, v.t. 1. To utter or pronounce written or printed words, letters or characters in the proper order.

2. To inspect and understand words or characters; to peruse silently.

3. To discover by marks; to understand; as, to read a man's countenance.

4. From Saxon raedan, to counsel, advise, discern; whence rede, counsel.

5. In Scripture, they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, Neh. 8; understandest thou what thou readest? Acts 8.

Key Scripture

Nehemiah 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

Deuteronomy 17:19 — "And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:"

Luke 4:16 — "And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read."

Acts 8:30 — "And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?"

Modern Corruption

Reading is redefined as an act in which the reader creates the meaning, so that the text has as many senses as it has readers; and against this, some react by denying that the sense ever needs to be given at all.

expand to see more

Postmodern literary theory teaches that a text has no fixed sense apart from the reader, and that every reading is finally an act of power. Reader-response criticism carried this into the church, where it now appears in the small-group question “what does this verse mean to you?” — a question that, taken seriously, abolishes the possibility of being wrong. Scripture assumes throughout that a text has a sense the reader is answerable to: Philip asks the eunuch, “Understandest thou what thou readest?” and the eunuch confesses that he cannot without a guide. Nehemiah 8:8 sets the standard against which the modern practice is measured — they read the text, and then they gave the sense, which presupposes that the text has one and that it can be missed. The Reformation principle of the plain sense is not naivety about difficulty; it is the confession that God spoke in order to be understood.

The opposite error deserves naming too, because it grows in reaction. Some insist that the plain reading is so plain that no teaching, no study of the original tongues, and no help from the church of past ages is needed, and that any explanation is a human addition. But God gave teachers as a gift to the church, and the same chapter that commands the reading commands that the sense be given. The principle to recover holds both together: the text is public, its sense is real and findable, and God has appointed men to open it — who are themselves to be tested by it, as the Bereans tested Paul.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qara', to call, cry, proclaim, and so to read aloud; Greek anaginōskō, to know again, to read; anagnōsis, the public reading.

expand to see more

Hebrew qara' (H7121) — to call out, proclaim, name, and hence to read aloud; the ordinary word for public reading of the law.

Hebrew miqra' (H4744) — a calling together, a convocation, and in later Hebrew the Scripture itself as that which is read.

Greek anaginōskō (G314) — to read; literally to know again, to recognise what another has written.

Greek anagnōsis (G320) — the reading; “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1 Timothy 4:13).

Aramaic qera' (H7123) — to read or call; used of the wise men who could not read the writing on Belshazzar's wall (Daniel 5:8).

Usage

"Of public reading with exposition: they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense (Nehemiah 8:8)."

"Of the ruler bound to the book: he shall read therein all the days of his life (Deuteronomy 17:19)."

"Of reading that needs a guide: Understandest thou what thou readest? (Acts 8:30)."
